source: a hand-maintained platform-settings inventory, cross-checked control by control against live repository state via gh api GETs; every desired value below equals a state that was verified live rather than written from memory
notes: projection is a jq filter applied to the read endpoint response; it extracts exactly the fields this baseline governs, so server-added defaults never cause false drift
desired is the expected projection output; comparison is done on canonical JSON (sorted keys, compact separators)
apply_payload is sent with --input - as the request body; controls without a payload send an empty body

apply_preserve is a jq filter read from the live read endpoint and merged into apply_payload before the corrective call: it carries forward fields the API requires in the body but the baseline deliberately does not govern

desired-state, not a minimum floor: a live setting stricter than the baseline is reported as drift, and for rulesets it is protected by the stricter-than-baseline guard (override with scripts/bootstrap.py --force-normalize)

applicability public: free-plan personal accounts only get this control on public repos (rulesets need GitHub Pro on private repos; code scanning, secret scanning and private vulnerability reporting are public-only without paid add-ons)
machine-local git signing config (docs/repo-settings.md, commit signing section) is out of scope: it is not a repository platform setting reachable through the API

a setting whose stricter value is the live one is deliberately NOT governed: the baseline must never be the reason a repository becomes less secure (see actions-workflow-permissions, and the secret-scanning validity-check and non-provider-pattern toggles left ungoverned for the same reason)

scope repo (the default) means the control is keyed by OWNER/REPO and its endpoints carry {repo}; scope org means it is keyed by an organization login and its endpoints carry {org}. Loading validates that a template carries exactly the placeholder its scope requires, so an organization control can never aim at a repository endpoint

manual_reason marks a control the REST API cannot correct: it is audited like any other, reports drift, and refuses to apply with that reason instead of claiming a successful write. Such a control carries no apply_method and no apply_endpoint

controls.description: Default branch ruleset: PR required (0 approvals), force-push and deletion blocked, signed commits required, no bypass actors
controls.projection: {bypass_actors, conditions, enforcement, name, pr: ([.rules[] | select(.type=="pull_request") | .parameters | {dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push, require_code_owner_review, require_last_push_approval, required_approving_review_count, required_review_thread_resolution}][0]), rule_types: ([.rules[].type] | sort), target}

controls.description: Tag ruleset for refs/tags/v*: deletion, update and force-update blocked; creation stays allowed for release automation
controls.projection: {bypass_actors, conditions, enforcement, name, rule_types: ([.rules[].type] | sort), target}

controls.description: Published releases and their assets can no longer be modified or deleted
CodeQL code scanning, GitHub-managed default setup, default query suite, weekly schedule
controls.applicability_note: also requires at least one CodeQL-supported language, probed live through na_when
controls.na_reason: no CodeQL-supported language in this repository
controls.na_note: the languages field of this endpoint is CodeQL's own list of what it can analyse, and it is populated whether or not default setup is configured; the repos/{repo}/languages endpoint reports linguist file types (Shell, Just, Dockerfile) that CodeQL does not analyse, so it would keep a docs-only or shell-only repository in permanent drift

controls.description: Dependabot vulnerability alerts enabled
Dependabot security updates (automated security fixes) enabled
GitHub secret scanning enabled
Secret scanning push protection enabled
Private vulnerability reporting enabled (the SECURITY.md reporting path)

Default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions read-only. can_approve_pull_request_reviews is deliberately NOT governed: forcing it true would loosen GitHub's stricter default on every repo. The corrective call preserves the live value (repos using release-please need it true - set it per repo).

Squash is the only merge method. Rebase merging is actively unsafe here: it rewrites commits without re-signing them, so under the required_signatures rule a rebase merge produces commits the rule rejects. Squash merging produces one GitHub-signed commit; merge commits would leave unsigned branch commits in the default branch history.
Merged pull-request branches are deleted automatically, so a stale branch cannot be revived and re-merged later

Wiki and projects disabled. A wiki is a second git repository that branch rules and rulesets do not cover, so leaving it on keeps an ungoverned write surface attached to a governed repository. Issues stay enabled: they carry the issue templates and disabling them would remove the documented reporting path.

Commits authored through the GitHub web editor must carry a sign-off. Repository-level mirror of the organization setting: the org value only covers repositories inside the org, so governing it here also catches repositories owned directly by a user.

Organization floor for every repository, present and future: force-push and deletion blocked on the default branch. Targets ~ALL rather than a tier, because preventing destruction is the floor every repository gets; the tier only adds process on top. Enforcement and the bypass list are projected, so flipping the ruleset to evaluate or granting a bypass actor is reported as drift.
controls.projection: {bypass_actors, conditions, enforcement, name, rule_types: ([.rules[].type] | sort), target}

controls.description: Organization floor for every repository: version tags cannot be deleted, moved or force-updated. Creation stays allowed so release automation still tags. A published version tag is a supply-chain artifact, so checksums and attestations only mean something if the tag naming them cannot move afterwards; that holds however casual the repository is, which is why this targets ~ALL and not the mature tier.
controls.projection: {bypass_actors, conditions, enforcement, name, rule_types: ([.rules[].type] | sort), target}

controls.description: Strict tier: repositories carrying the custom property tier=mature require a pull request (0 approvals, matching the single-maintainer model) and signed commits. Targeting a repository property rather than ~ALL is what lets sandbox repositories join the organization, inherit the security configuration and the destruction floor, and still take direct pushes. The pull-request parameters are projected field by field so the server-added allowed_merge_methods and required_reviewers defaults never read as drift.
controls.projection: {bypass_actors, conditions, enforcement, name, pr: ([.rules[] | select(.type=="pull_request") | .parameters | {dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push, require_code_owner_review, require_last_push_approval, required_approving_review_count, required_review_thread_resolution}][0]), rule_types: ([.rules[].type] | sort), target}

controls.description: The tier custom property that the strict ruleset selects on. values_editable_by org_actors is load-bearing: without it a repository administrator could promote or demote their own repository and opt out of the strict tier. required with default sandbox means every repository carries a value from the moment it exists, so a new repository is covered by the floor immediately and is never strict by accident. allowed_values is sorted in the projection so a reordering in the API response is not read as drift.
controls.projection: [.[] | select(.property_name=="tier") | {allowed_values: (.allowed_values | sort), default_value, property_name, required, value_type, values_editable_by}][0]

controls.description: The fld-forge-baseline security configuration is the organization default for every new repository and is enforced, so a repository administrator cannot disable the features it controls. Read through the plural defaults endpoint: the singular .../defaults path 404s, and the configurations list reports default_for_new_repos as null even when a default is set, so only this endpoint answers the question truthfully.
controls.manual_reason: creating a security configuration and attaching it as the default is a multi-step operation (create the configuration, then set it as default, then attach existing repositories) whose configuration id is organization-specific; this baseline audits the result and deliberately does not automate the correction

controls.description: Actions must reference a full commit SHA, organization-wide. Only sha_pinning_required is governed: allowed_actions is deliberately left ungoverned because pinning an allow-list here would force a stricter organization back to all, and an allow-listed action referenced by a mutable tag is still repointable, so SHA pinning is the control that actually prevents the attack. The corrective call preserves the live allowed_actions and enabled_repositories, which the endpoint requires in the body.

Default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions read-only across the organization. can_approve_pull_request_reviews is governed as true here, which looks like the opposite of the repository control that deliberately leaves it alone: at organization level this value is a ceiling, not a preference. A repository may be more restrictive than its organization but never less, so leaving it false here would make it impossible for any repository to turn it on, and release-please running under GITHUB_TOKEN would fail with 'GitHub Actions is not permitted to create or approve pull requests'. The per-repository desired state stays governed by actions-workflow-permissions, which preserves the live value instead of forcing it.

Workflow artifacts and logs are kept 30 days, matching the retention-days the fleet's CI already declares on its uploads so one number governs both. The organization value is a hard cap every repository inherits. Accepted trade-off: a supply-chain problem found more than 30 days late loses its workflow-log trail, while immutable releases with attestations, signed commits and alert history do not expire with it.

Member privileges the REST API can both read and write: members cannot create repositories or teams, base permission on organization repositories is read, private forks are off, issue deletion is off, and web-editor commits carry a sign-off. Organization owners are exempt from the creation restrictions by design, so agents acting with the owner's token can still create repositories.

Member privileges the REST API reports but refuses to change: deleting repositories, changing repository visibility and inviting outside collaborators should all be owner-only. Auditing them here turns three lines of a manual checklist into an audited item that reports drift until someone actually clears it.
controls.manual_reason: web UI only: a PATCH carrying these fields returns 200 and silently keeps the old value. Clear them under Organization settings > Member privileges

controls.description: Two-factor authentication required for every member. A compromised member account without it is a compromise of the whole fleet, so this is audited as true even though only the web UI can set it: the audit becomes the standing reminder until it is done.
controls.manual_reason: web UI only: the field is readable but not an accepted PATCH parameter. Enable it under Organization settings > Authentication security, after checking that 'gh api orgs/{org}/members?filter=2fa_disabled' lists nobody, because enabling it removes every member without 2FA
